title: Staying Safe in the Sun
summary: How the Sun helps us, how its invisible UV rays and heat can harm skin, eyes, and the body, and simple ways to stay protected.
poll: Sunscreen is only needed at the beach.

versions.title: Safe in the Sun
versions.text:
The Sun is bright and hot. It gives us light. It helps plants grow. It helps your body, too.

But the Sun sends out rays you can not see. These rays can hurt your skin. Too much sun can burn you. A sunburn is red and sore. It can hurt for days.

The rays can hurt your eyes, too. Do not look right at the Sun!

The Sun is strong in the middle of the day. Look at your shadow. Is it short? Then the Sun is strong.

How can you stay safe? Play in the shade. Shade is a cool spot out of the sun. A tree makes shade.

Put on sunscreen. It is a cream that helps block the rays. Put on more when you swim.

Wear a hat. Wear sunglasses. Long sleeves help, too.

Hot days can make you feel sick. Drink lots of water. Rest when you feel too hot.

Clouds do not stop all the rays. Sand and water can bounce them back at you. So be safe on the beach, too.

versions.title: Staying Safe in the Sun
versions.text:
The Sun is bright and powerful. It gives us light and warmth, it helps plants grow, and it even helps your body stay healthy.

However, the Sun also sends out invisible rays that can harm your skin. Too much sun can give you a sunburn, which makes skin red, sore, and painful for days. Over many years, too much sun can lead to serious skin problems.

These rays can damage your eyes as well. Never look directly at the Sun!

The Sun is strongest in the middle of the day. Here is a simple trick. Look at your shadow. If your shadow is shorter than you are, the Sun's rays are strong.

How can you stay safe? First, play in the shade. Shade is a cool place out of direct sunlight, such as the space under a tree or an umbrella.

Third, wear a hat, sunglasses, and light clothes with long sleeves.

Hot days can also make you feel sick and dizzy. Drink plenty of water, and rest when you feel too hot.

Remember that clouds do not block all the rays. Sand and water can bounce rays back at you, so stay careful at the beach.

versions.title: Staying Safe in the Sun
versions.text:
The Sun is a wonderful neighbor. It gives us light and warmth, it helps plants grow, and it even helps our bodies make vitamin D, which keeps bones strong. But the Sun can also be harmful if we are not careful.

Along with light we can see, the Sun sends out invisible rays called ultraviolet rays, or UV rays. UV rays can damage the skin. A sunburn is a sign of this damage. It makes the skin red, sore, and painful. Over many years, too much sun can cause wrinkles and even skin cancer.

UV rays can also harm the eyes, so you should never look directly at the Sun.

UV rays are strongest from about 10 in the morning to 4 in the afternoon. A simple trick can help you check. If your shadow is shorter than you are, the rays are strong.

There are many ways to protect yourself. Stay in the shade when you can. Use sunscreen and put on more every two hours, especially after swimming. Wear a wide hat, sunglasses, and loose, light clothes that cover your arms.

Heat is another danger. On hot days, your body loses water through sweat. Losing too much water is called dehydration, and it can make you feel tired, dizzy, and sick. Drink water often, even before you feel thirsty.

Finally, remember that clouds do not block all UV rays. Sand and water also reflect rays back toward you, so you need protection at the beach, too.

versions.title: Protecting Yourself from the Sun
versions.text:
The Sun is an essential neighbor. It provides light and warmth, it allows plants to grow, and it even helps our bodies produce vitamin D, which keeps bones strong. However, the Sun can also be harmful if we are careless.

Along with visible light, the Sun gives off invisible rays called ultraviolet rays, or UV rays. These rays can damage the skin, and a sunburn is a clear sign of that damage, leaving the skin red, sore, and painful. Over many years, too much sun exposure can cause wrinkles and even skin cancer.

UV rays can also injure the eyes, so you should never look directly at the Sun.

UV rays are most intense from about 10 in the morning until 4 in the afternoon. A simple trick can help you check: if your shadow is shorter than you are, the rays are especially strong.

There are several ways to protect yourself. Stay in the shade whenever possible. Apply sunscreen about fifteen minutes before going outside, and reapply it every two hours, especially after swimming. Wear a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses that block UV rays, and loose, light-colored clothing that covers your arms. In fact, the traditional head coverings and long, loose robes worn in Saudi Arabia are excellent protection from the desert sun.

Heat presents another danger. On hot days, your body loses water through sweat. Losing too much water is called dehydration, and it can make you feel tired, dizzy, and sick. Drink water regularly, even before you feel thirsty, and if you ever feel faint, move to a cool place and tell an adult immediately.

Finally, remember that clouds do not block all UV rays. Sand and water also reflect rays back toward you, so you need protection at the beach as well.

versions.title: Sunlight, Safety, and Your Health
versions.text:
The Sun functions, in effect, as an indispensable celestial neighbor: it supplies the light and warmth that sustain plant growth across the planet, and it even enables the human body to manufacture vitamin D, a nutrient essential for maintaining robust bone strength. Nevertheless, the identical sunlight that makes life on Earth possible can also inflict genuine harm whenever it is treated with insufficient caution or its power is simply underestimated.

Alongside the visible light we readily perceive, the Sun additionally emits a form of invisible radiation known as ultraviolet rays, or UV rays, which possess the capacity to damage the skin at a cellular level. A sunburn constitutes an unmistakable, immediate indication of such damage, leaving the affected skin red, tender, and painful, while repeated exposure sustained across many years can produce premature wrinkling and, in more severe cases, skin cancer. Because UV radiation can likewise injure the eyes, one should never look directly toward the Sun, even for the briefest instant.

Ultraviolet radiation reaches its greatest intensity during the interval extending roughly from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon. Weather forecasts frequently incorporate a UV index, a standardized numerical scale indicating the anticipated strength of these rays, and during a typical Saudi summer this index regularly attains eleven or higher, a category formally classified as extreme. A simple, practical observation provides additional confirmation: whenever one's shadow appears shorter than one's own height, the surrounding radiation is likely to be especially intense and correspondingly hazardous.

Fortunately, several effective strategies exist for mitigating this risk, beginning with remaining within shaded areas whenever circumstances permit. Sunscreen should be applied approximately fifteen minutes prior to venturing outdoors and reapplied at roughly two-hour intervals, particularly following swimming or episodes of profuse perspiration. Dermatologists generally recommend selecting a broad-spectrum product offering a sun protection factor, or SPF, of at least thirty. One should additionally wear a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses engineered specifically to block UV radiation, and loose-fitting, light-colored garments that cover the arms, since the traditional head coverings and long, flowing robes customarily worn throughout Saudi Arabia furnish genuinely excellent protection against the intense desert sun.

Heat introduces an additional and distinct hazard, since on particularly hot days the body loses considerable quantities of water through perspiration, and the excessive loss of bodily water is formally termed dehydration, a condition capable of inducing exhaustion, dizziness, and nausea in short order. It is therefore advisable to drink water consistently, even preemptively, before any sensation of thirst actually develops, and anyone who begins to feel faint should immediately relocate to a cool, shaded environment and inform a responsible adult without delay.

Finally, it bears emphasizing that clouds fail to block the majority of UV rays, and that both sand and water actively reflect additional radiation back toward the body, meaning that adequate protective measures remain essential even at the beach or within the open desert on seemingly overcast days.

Nevertheless, the identical sunlight that renders life on Earth possible can also inflict genuine physiological harm whenever it is treated with insufficient caution or its cumulative power is simply underestimated over time.

Alongside the visible light that the human eye readily perceives, the Sun additionally emits a category of invisible radiation known as ultraviolet rays, or UV rays, which possess the capacity to damage skin tissue at a cellular level, disrupting the genetic material within individual cells. A sunburn constitutes an unmistakable, immediate indication of such cellular damage, leaving the affected skin red, tender, and painful, while repeated exposure sustained across many years can produce premature wrinkling and, in more severe instances, skin cancer. Because UV radiation can likewise inflict serious injury upon the eyes, one should never look directly toward the Sun under any circumstances, even for the briefest conceivable instant.

Ultraviolet radiation attains its greatest intensity during the interval extending roughly from ten in the morning until four in the afternoon, when the Sun's rays strike the Earth's surface most directly. Weather forecasts frequently incorporate a UV index, a standardized numerical scale indicating the anticipated strength of ambient radiation, and during a typical Saudi summer this index regularly attains eleven or higher, a category formally classified by meteorologists as extreme. A simple, practical observation provides additional, readily accessible confirmation: whenever one's shadow appears shorter than one's own physical height, the surrounding radiation is almost certainly especially intense and correspondingly hazardous to unprotected skin.

Fortunately, several demonstrably effective strategies exist for mitigating this cumulative risk, beginning with remaining within shaded areas whenever circumstances reasonably permit. Sunscreen should be applied approximately fifteen minutes prior to venturing outdoors and systematically reapplied at roughly two-hour intervals, particularly following swimming or episodes of profuse perspiration that might otherwise wash the protective layer away. Dermatologists generally recommend selecting a broad-spectrum product offering a sun protection factor, or SPF, of at least thirty. One should additionally wear a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses engineered specifically to block UV radiation, and loose-fitting, light-colored garments that cover the arms and shoulders, since the traditional head coverings and long, flowing robes customarily worn throughout Saudi Arabia furnish genuinely excellent protection against the intense desert sun.

Heat introduces an additional and physiologically distinct hazard, since on particularly hot days the body loses considerable quantities of water through perspiration, and the excessive, uncompensated loss of bodily fluid is formally termed dehydration, a condition capable of inducing exhaustion, dizziness, and nausea with surprising rapidity. It is therefore advisable to drink water consistently and preemptively, well before any conscious sensation of thirst actually develops, and anyone who begins to feel faint should immediately relocate to a cool, shaded environment and inform a responsible adult without any delay whatsoever.

Finally, it bears particular emphasis that clouds fail to block the overwhelming majority of UV rays, and that both sand and water actively reflect substantial additional radiation back toward the body from below, meaning that rigorous protective measures remain essential even at the beach or within the open desert on seemingly overcast days when the danger is easily, and dangerously, underestimated.

questions.stem: Which person is best protected from the Sun?
options: Ali, swimming at noon with no hat
Huda, sitting on bright sand at 1 p.m.
Omar, wearing a wide hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen in the shade
Laila, playing on a cloudy beach without sunscreen
questions.why: Omar follows several pieces of advice: shade, hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen.

wrong.A: Noon is a time of strong UV rays, and he has no hat.
wrong.B: Sand reflects rays, and 1 p.m. is a strong-sun time.
wrong.D: Clouds do not block all UV rays.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the part about staying safe?
options: By listing several ways to protect yourself
By telling a story about a trip to the beach
By comparing the Sun with the Moon
By describing events from long ago
questions.why: The article lists protective steps: shade, sunscreen, hats, sunglasses, clothing, and drinking water.

wrong.B: There is no story about a trip.
wrong.D: The article does not describe history.

MID.prompt: Explain two dangers of the Sun and how a person can protect against each one. Use details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: One danger of the sun is ultraviolet rays, which can damage your skin and cause a sunburn; you can protect yourself by staying in the shade and wearing sunscreen. Another danger is dehydration, because your body loses water through sweat on hot days, so drinking water often can protect against it. I also learned that sand and water reflect rays back at you, so protection is still needed at the beach.

keyWords.definition: describing invisible radiation from the Sun that can damage skin and eyes
keyWords.example: The scientist used a special lamp that gives off ultraviolet light.

keyWords.definition: a number or scale that shows the level of something
keyWords.example: The air-quality index was high, so we stayed indoors.

keyWords.definition: a harmful condition in which the body lacks enough water
keyWords.example: Marathon runners drink often to avoid dehydration.

keyWords.definition: to throw back light, heat, or sound from a surface
keyWords.example: Snow can reflect so much light that skiers wear dark goggles.
Air is invisible, but we can feel it when the wind blows.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Sunlight is both beneficial and potentially harmful, so people should take sensible precautions.
Sunscreen is the only protection anyone needs.
UV rays are visible on cloudy days.
Vitamin D causes sunburn.
questions.why: The article balances the Sun's benefits with its dangers and explains several precautions.

wrong.B: The article recommends shade, clothing, sunglasses, and water as well.
wrong.D: Vitamin D is a benefit, not a cause of sunburn.

questions.stem: According to the article, what does a UV index of 11 or higher mean?
options: The rays are very weak.
The Sun has set.
The rays are at the extreme level.
It is safe to stay outside all day.
questions.why: The article says that in a Saudi summer the index often reaches 11 or higher, the extreme level.

wrong.A: A high number means strong rays.
wrong.D: An extreme level calls for more protection.

questions.stem: When does the article say sunscreen should first be applied?
options: After you get a sunburn
About fifteen minutes before going outside
Only after swimming
At night, just before going to sleep in bed
questions.why: The article advises applying sunscreen about fifteen minutes before going out.

wrong.A: Sunscreen is meant to prevent sunburn.
wrong.C: Reapplying after swimming is extra advice, not the first use.
wrong.D: Sunscreen is for time spent in the Sun.

questions.stem: The article describes UV rays as invisible. This word suggests that the rays —
options: cannot reach the ground
are only present at night, after the Sun sets
are colorful and bright
cannot be seen, so their danger is easy to forget
questions.why: Invisible means unable to be seen, which is why people may not notice the danger.

wrong.A: They reach the ground and can cause sunburn.
wrong.C: Invisible rays cannot be seen at all.

questions.stem: According to the article, what can repeated sun exposure over many years lead to?
options: Stronger eyesight and healthier, brighter eyes
Premature wrinkles and even skin cancer
More vitamin D than the body can use
A higher UV index
questions.why: The article states that excessive sun exposure over many years can cause premature wrinkles and even skin cancer.

wrong.A: UV rays can injure the eyes.
wrong.C: The article does not mention this.
wrong.D: The index measures the Sun's strength, not a person's exposure.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention traditional head coverings and long, loose robes worn in Saudi Arabia?
options: To show that familiar clothing already offers good sun protection
To describe fashion trends
To suggest that sunscreen is unnecessary for anyone who wears robes
To explain how the UV index is measured
questions.why: The author connects the advice about covering skin to clothing readers already know.

wrong.B: The point is protection, not fashion.
wrong.D: Clothing is unrelated to how the index is measured.

questions.stem: Why might a person get sunburned at the beach even on a cloudy day?
options: Clouds increase the Sun's heat.
UV rays pass through clouds and are also reflected by sand and water.
Sea water contains UV rays.
Sunscreen stops working completely whenever it is near the ocean.
questions.why: The article says clouds do not block all UV rays, and sand and water reflect them toward you.

wrong.A: The article does not say clouds add heat.
wrong.C: Water reflects rays; it does not contain them.
wrong.D: The article says to reapply after swimming, not that it stops working.

questions.stem: Which conclusion can be drawn from the shadow trick?
options: The higher the Sun is in the sky, the stronger the UV rays tend to be.
Shadows protect people from UV rays.
Tall people need less sunscreen.
UV rays are strongest at sunrise.
questions.why: Short shadows happen when the Sun is high, and the article says that is when rays are especially strong.

wrong.B: A shadow is only a sign of the Sun's angle.
wrong.C: Height does not change how much protection you need.
wrong.D: The article says rays are strongest from about 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

HIGH.prompt: The article says the same sunlight that supports life can also be harmful. Explain this idea, using at least three pieces of evidence from the text.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The article shows that the same sun that helps us also has a hidden danger. Sunlight gives us light and warmth and even helps our bodies make vitamin D, but it also sends out invisible ultraviolet rays that can damage the skin and cause sunburn, wrinkles, or even skin cancer over time. Heat from the sun can also cause dehydration, since the body loses water through sweat on hot days. Even surfaces like sand and water reflect ultraviolet rays back at you, which is why protection is still necessary even in the shade or on a cloudy day.
